stem: At the start of an experiment, the pressure inside a container was 19 pounds per square inch (psi). The pressure inside the container doubled every 28 minutes after the start of the experiment. Which equation represents this situation, where y is the pressure, in psi, inside the container x minutes after the start of the experiment?
whyCorrect: Exponential growth is written as (starting value)(growth factor) raised to (elapsed time divided by the length of one growth period). The starting value is 19 and the growth factor is 2 because the pressure doubles. One doubling period is 28 minutes, so after x minutes the number of doublings is \( \frac{x}{28} \) , giving \( y = 19(2)^{\frac{x}{28}} \) . Check it: at x = 28 the exponent is 1 and the pressure is 38, exactly double.

whyWrong.B: This makes 28 the growth factor and 2x the exponent. At x = 28 it gives 19 times 28 to the 56th power, not one doubling.
whyWrong.C: This is a quadratic in x, not an exponential. At x = 0 it gives 19(28)^2 = 14,896 psi instead of the stated 19 psi.
whyWrong.D: This is also quadratic, and at x = 0 it gives 28 psi rather than 19; nothing in it ever doubles on a fixed schedule.

stem: For a study, a research team measured the heights of 380 king penguins from the Kerguelen Islands and 190 king penguins from the Falkland Islands. The research team determined that the mean height of the 380 king penguins from the Kerguelen Islands was 87 centimeters and the mean height of the 190 king penguins from the Falkland Islands was 93 centimeters. What was the mean height, in centimeters, of all 570 king penguins the research team measured for this study?
whyCorrect: You cannot average two means unless the groups are the same size, and here one group is twice the other. Rebuild the totals instead: 380 × 87 = 33,060 and 190 × 93 = 17,670, so all 570 penguins total 50,730 centimeters. Dividing, 50,730 ÷ 570 = 89. The answer sits closer to 87 than to 93 because the 87-centimeter group is twice as large.

whyWrong.A: 91 is what you get by weighting the groups backwards, as though the Falkland group were the larger one.
whyWrong.C: 90 is the plain average of 87 and 93, which ignores that the Kerguelen group has twice as many penguins.
whyWrong.D: 88 is a guess pulled one unit off 87; the two-to-one weighting moves the mean two units, not one.

stem:
a, 26, 29, b, 31, 47, c

For the given data set, the data values are listed in ascending order, where a, b, and c are constants. For this data set, the mean is 36, the median is 29, and the range is 72. What is the value of c?
whyCorrect: Start with the median, because it pins down a value directly: seven values in ascending order put the median in the 4th position, which is b, so b = 29. Now the mean gives a + 26 + 29 + 29 + 31 + 47 + c = 7 × 36 = 252, so a + c = 90. The list is ascending, so a is the smallest and c the largest and the range gives c − a = 72. Adding the two equations, 2c = 162, so c = 81 (and a = 9, which does sit below 26 as required).

whyWrong.A: 54 comes from subtracting the mean from the sum, 90 − 36, instead of solving a + c = 90 together with c − a = 72.
whyWrong.B: 72 is the range itself, not the largest value. The range is a difference, and the smallest value a is 9, not 0.
whyWrong.D: 98 comes from treating 26 as the smallest value and adding the range to it: 26 + 72. But a sits below 26 in the list, so a, not 26, is the minimum.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit for the data is also shown. For how many of the 9 data points is the actual y-value greater than the y-value predicted by the line of best fit?
whyCorrect: "Predicted" means the height of the line directly above or below that point's own x-value, so compare each point vertically with the line, not with the other points. The line runs from about (0.5, 80) up to about (10, 100). Going left to right, the points near x = 1, 2, 3, 4.5 and 9 sit above the line and the points near x = 5, 6, 7 and 8.5 sit below it. That is 5 points above.

whyWrong.A: 8 counts every point that is above y = 80, the line's starting height, instead of above the line at that point's own x. The line rises to 100, so being above 80 is not enough.
whyWrong.B: 7 comes from missing the two points on the right that sit just below the rising line; near x = 7 and x = 8.5 the line has already climbed past them.
whyWrong.D: 2 counts only the points that clear the line by an obvious margin. Three more points on the left are above it by a smaller amount and still count.

stem: The graph shows the number of internet users worldwide y, in billions, x years after 2007. Which of the following is closest to the number of internet users worldwide, in billions, 5 years after 2007?
whyCorrect: x is years after 2007, so "5 years after 2007" is x = 5, not the fifth plotted point counting from the left of a list. Go up from 5 on the horizontal axis to the point there and read across: it sits just under halfway between 2 and 3, about 2.4 billion.

whyWrong.A: 1.4 is the value at x = 0, that is, in 2007 itself.
whyWrong.C: 3.4 is higher than any plotted point; even at x = 9 the graph has only reached about 3.1.
whyWrong.D: 4.4 is well off the data, which never rises above about 3.

stem: The scatterplot shows data set A, which consists of the weights y, in pounds, of a Labrador retriever puppy at various ages, x, in months. The equation of a line of best fit for the relationship in data set A can be written as \( y = -5.1 + 8.7x \) , where \( 2 \le x \le 6 \) . The puppy was weighed again at 9 months old and weighed 52 pounds. Data set B consists of all the data points in data set A as well as the data point (9, 52). The equation of a line of best fit for data set B can be written as \( y = r + sx \) , where r and s are constants and \( 2 \le x \le 9 \) . Assuming the equations of the lines of best fit are calculated in the same way, which of the following is the best estimate for the value of s?
whyCorrect: s is the slope of the new line, so ask what the extra point does to the trend rather than trying to recompute a regression. Data set A's line predicts \( -5.1 + 8.7(9) = 73.2 \) pounds at 9 months, but the puppy actually weighed 52 pounds — far below the trend, and at the far right where it pulls hardest. A point that low on the right end drags the right side of the line down, so the new slope must be smaller than 8.7. Only 5.9 is smaller.

whyWrong.B: 8.7 is the old slope, which would only stay the same if the new point landed on the old line. It lands 21 pounds below it.
whyWrong.C: 13.8 is a steeper slope, which would require the new point to sit above the old line, not below it.
whyWrong.D: 17.7 is roughly double the old slope; nothing here makes the growth trend steeper. It also comes from dividing 52 by 3 or similar, which is not a slope.

note: The book prints the domains with the inequality signs reversed (2 ≥ x ≥ 6 and 2 ≥ x ≥ 9), which is impossible; transcribed as 2 ≤ x ≤ 6 and 2 ≤ x ≤ 9. The book also writes the new line as y = r + st, using t where the variable is x.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following equations best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: The plotted line clearly rises from left to right, so its equation must contain an x term with a positive coefficient. Only one choice does. The others describe horizontal lines or are not equations at all, so no reading of the graph is needed beyond noticing the line is not flat.

whyWrong.A: y = 0 is the horizontal x-axis; the line shown is neither horizontal nor on the axis.
whyWrong.B: y = 1.7 is a horizontal line at height 1.7. A constant y cannot describe a line that climbs.
whyWrong.C: 0.7 is a number, not an equation, so it cannot represent any line. It is the slope-shaped part of choice D with the rest removed.

note: The line drawn in the figure passes close to the origin, so its y-intercept looks nearer 0 than the 1.7 in choice D; D is still the only choice that is an increasing linear equation. Choice C is printed without "y =".

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between t and d, along with a line of best fit. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: Every choice has the same slope, so the slope tells you nothing — only the constant separates them. Test one point instead: the data run from about (230, 400) to about (270, 490). Substituting t = 230 into choice A gives \( -62.1 + 2.02(230) \approx 402 \) , which matches. The graph never shows t = 0, so the constant is far below the plotted d-values rather than near them.

whyWrong.B: At t = 230 this predicts about 627, roughly 200 too high; nothing on the graph reaches that.
whyWrong.C: At t = 230 this predicts about 822, nearly double the observed value. 357.8 was read as though it were a d-value on the graph.
whyWrong.D: At t = 230 this predicts about 857. Like C, it treats the constant as the height of the line over the plotted region instead of its value at t = 0.

stem: For the first 10 hours of an experiment, the scatterplot shows the temperature y, in degrees Fahrenheit (°F), of an object at various times x, in hours, since the start of the experiment. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following is the best interpretation of the slope of the line of best fit?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The predicted temperature increases at a constant rate of approximately 40°F per hour over the 10-hour period.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The predicted temperature decreases at a constant rate of approximately 40°F per hour over the 10-hour period.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The predicted temperature decreases at a constant rate of approximately 180°F per hour over the 10-hour period.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The predicted temperature increases at a constant rate of approximately 180°F per hour over the 10-hour period.

whyCorrect: Two decisions: direction and size. The line rises left to right, so the rate is an increase, which rules out half the choices immediately. For the size, the line climbs from roughly 200°F at 0 hours to roughly 550°F at 10 hours, a rise of about 350°F over 10 hours, so about 35°F per hour — approximately 40.

whyWrong.B: The direction is wrong. A decrease would need the line to fall as time increases, and it rises.
whyWrong.C: Both parts are wrong: the line rises, and 180°F per hour would put the object above 1,800°F by hour 10.
whyWrong.D: The direction is right but the size is not. 180 is roughly the height of the line near the start, or its rise over 2 hours, not its rise per single hour.

stem: The scatterplot shows 5 measurements of the body length, in centimeters (cm), of a New Zealand fur seal from an age of 1 year to 6 years old. A line of best fit is also shown. For a New Zealand fur seal at an age of 3 years old, what is the body length predicted by the line of best fit, to the nearest 10 cm?
whyCorrect: The question asks for the line's value, not a data point's, and at age 3 there is no plotted point — that is the trap. Go up from 3 on the horizontal axis to the line itself and read across: the line is a little above 105, so to the nearest 10 cm the prediction is 110.

stem: The scatterplot shows 5 measurements of the body length, in centimeters (cm), of a New Zealand fur seal from an age of 1 year to 6 years old. A line of best fit is also shown. For a New Zealand fur seal at an age of 3 years old, what is the body length predicted by the line of best fit, to the nearest 10 cm?
whyCorrect: Read the line, not the points: at age 3 no seal was measured, so trace up from 3 to the line of best fit and across to the vertical axis. The line is just above 100 there, so to the nearest 10 cm the predicted length is 100 cm.
note: The book truncates the last words of the stem to "to the nearest ?"; the rounding unit is restored as 10 cm from the parallel question printed beside it. If a different unit was intended the answer changes.

A scatterplot has 13 data points that follow an exponential pattern trending up from left to right. The data points have the following approximate coordinates.

Which of the following equations is the most appropriate model for the data shown in the scatterplot?
whyCorrect: Use the two ends of the data. Far to the left the y-values flatten out near 19, so the model needs a constant term of about 18 — without one the curve would fall toward 0. Then use x = 0, where y = 24: for \( y = a(1.55)^{x} + 18 \) this gives a + 18 = 24, so a = 6. Checking the right end, \( 6(1.55)^{4} + 18 \approx 53 \) , which matches the observed 49 at x = 4.

whyWrong.A: With no constant term this drops toward 0 on the left, but the data level off near 19. At x = −4 it predicts about 4, not 19.
whyWrong.B: At x = 0 this gives 24 + 18 = 42, but the data show y = 24 there. The 24 belongs to a + c, not to a alone.
whyWrong.C: This has a coefficient of 1, so it barely grows: at x = 4 it predicts about 29 against an observed 49. It fits x = 0 by accident.

note: The scatterplot's data points are given as a coordinate list in the book, so the figure is reproduced here as a table.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between x and y for the 10 data points in data set A. Data set B is created by multiplying the y-value of each data point from data set A by 40. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate model for data set B?
whyCorrect: First model data set A itself: the points pass through about (0, 3), (2, 20), (3, 43) and (4, 100), which fits \( y = 5(2.04)^{x} \) . Multiplying every y-value by 40 scales the whole output, so it multiplies the coefficient in front, not the exponent or the base: \( 40 \times 5 = 200 \) , giving roughly \( y = 200(2.04)^{x} \) . Only one choice has a coefficient anywhere near 200.

whyWrong.A: This is the model for data set A itself, before the y-values were multiplied by 40.
whyWrong.B: This multiplies the wrong thing. Scaling y by 40 does not turn the coefficient 5 into 40, and it does not add a constant 40 either.
whyWrong.C: Adding 40 shifts every point up by 40; multiplying by 40 stretches them. At x = 4 data set B is near 4,000, and this predicts about 127.

note: Choice D carries a spurious additive 2.04; the exact transformed model is 200(2.04)^x, and D is the only choice with a coefficient of that size.

stem: The line graph shows the number of customers who visited a restaurant each day during a four-day period in the summer. According to the line graph, for which day during this four-day period did the restaurant have the smallest number of customers who visited?
whyCorrect: Smallest number of customers means the lowest point on the graph, not the leftmost or the shortest gap between points. The graph rises from left to right the whole way, so the lowest point is the first one, Day 1, at about 22 customers.

whyWrong.B: Day 2 is slightly higher than Day 1, at about 27. It is close, but the graph still climbs between the two.
whyWrong.C: Day 3 is around 47, well above the start.
whyWrong.D: Day 4 is the highest point, about 56 — the largest number of customers, not the smallest.

stem: A group of 10 gardeners recorded data on the germination rates of their tomato crop for one growing season. The scatterplot shows the relationship between the number of tomato seeds planted, x, and the number of tomato seeds that germinated, y, for each of the gardeners. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following is the best interpretation of the slope of the line of best fit in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The number of tomato seeds planted is predicted to increase by 60 seeds every 100 days.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The number of tomato seeds planted is predicted to increase by 300 seeds every 100 days.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The number of tomato seeds that germinate is predicted to increase by 60 seeds for every additional 100 tomato seeds that are planted.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The number of tomato seeds that germinate is predicted to increase by 300 seeds for every additional 100 tomato seeds that are planted.

whyCorrect: A slope always says how much the vertical variable changes per unit of the horizontal variable, so here it is germinated seeds per seed planted — time is not a variable in this graph at all. The line climbs from about 20 to about 310 as x goes from 0 to 500, a rise of roughly 290 over 500, or about 0.6. That is 60 germinated seeds for every extra 100 planted.

whyWrong.A: Days appear nowhere on the axes, and it also has the slope describing the horizontal variable rather than the vertical one.
whyWrong.B: Same two errors as A, with a slope of 3 on top of them.
whyWrong.D: A slope of 3 would mean more seeds germinate than were planted. The line rises less steeply than the 45-degree direction, so the slope is below 1.

stem: In the figure, line q is parallel to line r, and both are intersected by line s. If y = 2x + 7, what is the value of x?
whyCorrect: The 57° angle sits above line q on the right of the transversal, and y sits above line r on the left of it, so they are not the same angle. Slide 57° down to line r as a corresponding angle: the angle above r on the right is also 57°. y is its supplement along line r, so y = 180 − 57 = 123. Then 123 = 2x + 7 gives 2x = 116 and x = 58.

whyWrong.A: 25 comes from setting y = 57, treating the two labelled angles as equal. They are on opposite sides of the transversal, so they are supplementary, not equal.
whyWrong.B: 32 is 90 − 58, from assuming the two labelled angles are complementary.
whyWrong.D: 68 comes from solving 2x + 7 = 143 or similar; check the subtraction, 180 − 57 = 123, not 143.

stem: The measure of angle G is \( \frac{\pi}{10} \) radians. If the measure of angle G is 9n in degrees, where n is a constant, what is the value of n?
whyCorrect: Convert first, then solve. Since \( \pi \) radians is 180°, \( \frac{\pi}{10} \) radians is \( \frac{180}{10} = 18 \) degrees. The same angle is written as 9n degrees, so 9n = 18 and n = 2.

whyWrong.B: 9 is the coefficient already in the expression 9n, not the value of n.
whyWrong.C: 10 is the denominator of the radian measure; it is not what n multiplies out to.
whyWrong.D: 18 is the angle's measure in degrees. n is that measure divided by 9.

stem:
In the figure shown, line r is parallel to line s, and line t intersects both lines. What is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Only two different angle sizes exist in the whole figure, 121° and 59°, so the work is deciding which one x is. The 121° angle is above r on the left of t; its vertical angle, below r on the right of t, is also 121°. x sits below s on the right of t, the same position at the other parallel line, so it is a corresponding angle and equals 121.

whyWrong.B: 90 assumes t meets the parallel lines at a right angle. The marked angles are 121° and 59°, so it does not.
whyWrong.C: 31 is 90 − 59, treating the angles as complementary. Angles on a straight line are supplementary, so they pair to 180, not 90.
whyWrong.D: 180 is the full straight angle along line s, which is the sum of two of the four angles at that intersection, not one of them.

stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 36 inches. If the sum of the lengths of three sides of the rectangle is 21 inches, what is the length, in inches, of the fourth side?
whyCorrect: The perimeter is the sum of all four sides, so the fourth side is whatever is left after the other three: 36 − 21 = 15. You never need the individual length and width, which is the trap — setting up 2L + 2W = 36 wastes time here.

whyWrong.A: 3 is the other dimension of the rectangle, which is 3 by 15. It is a side, but not the one left out of the 21.
whyWrong.B: 57 comes from adding 36 and 21 instead of subtracting. The three sides are part of the perimeter, so the result must be smaller than 36.
whyWrong.D: 36 is the whole perimeter, which is all four sides together.

stem:
In the figure shown, lines r and s are parallel, and line t intersects both lines. What is the value of a?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: a sits above line s on the right of t, which is the same position as the 77° angle above line r on the right of t. Parallel lines cut by a transversal make those corresponding angles equal, so a = 77. You can also get there along line s: the 77° below s on the left is vertical to a.

whyWrong.A: 180 is the straight angle along line s, the sum of a and the angle beside it, not a itself.
whyWrong.C: 167 is not the measure of any angle here; every angle in the figure is either 77° or 103°.
whyWrong.D: 90 would require t to be perpendicular to the parallel lines, but the marked angles are 77° and 103°.

stem: The measure of angle K is \( \frac{\pi}{2(12)} \) radians. The measure of angle L is 12 times the measure of angle K. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle L?
whyCorrect: Convert K to degrees before multiplying. Since \( \pi \) radians is 180°, \( \frac{\pi}{2(12)} = \frac{\pi}{24} \) radians is \( \frac{180}{24} = 7.5 \) degrees. Twelve times that is 90°. A shortcut: multiplying \( \frac{\pi}{24} \) by 12 gives \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) , and a half-turn of \( \pi \) is 180°, so a quarter of a turn is 90°.

whyWrong.A: 102 is 90 + 12, adding the multiplier instead of applying it.
whyWrong.B: 12 is how many times bigger L is than K, not a measure in degrees.
whyWrong.C: 78 is 90 − 12, subtracting the multiplier.

note: An unrelated display line, a/(b + c) = 55, is printed above this question in the book; it belongs to a neighbouring item and is not part of the stem.

stem: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, where angle A corresponds to angle D and angle C corresponds to angle F. Angles C and F are right angles. If \( \tan A = \frac{612}{35} \) , what is the value of \( \sin D \) ?
whyCorrect: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles, so \( \sin D = \sin A \) and you can work entirely inside triangle ABC. With the right angle at C, \( \tan A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{612}{35} \) , so take the legs as 612 and 35 and find the hypotenuse: \( \sqrt{612^{2} + 35^{2}} = \sqrt{375{,}769} = 613 \) . Then \( \sin A = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{612}{613} \) .

whyWrong.B: \( \frac{35}{613} \) is \( \cos A \) , the sine of the other acute angle. Sine uses the leg across from the angle, and 35 is the leg beside it.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{613}{612} \) is the reciprocal of the answer; the hypotenuse belongs in the denominator, since a sine can never exceed 1.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{613}{35} \) is the reciprocal of the cosine, and again greater than 1.

stem:
In the figure, lines r and s are parallel and line t intersects both lines. If \( a = 4k + 57 \) and \( b = \frac{k}{2} + 55 \) , what is the value of c?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Place the three angles first. a and b are both between the parallel lines and both on the same side of t, so they are same-side interior angles and a + b = 180. b and c share line s, so they are a linear pair and b + c = 180 — which makes c equal to a. Solving \( (4k + 57) + \left(\frac{k}{2} + 55\right) = 180 \) gives \( \frac{9k}{2} = 68 \) , so \( k = \frac{136}{9} \) and \( c = a = 4k + 57 = \frac{1057}{9} \approx 117.44 \) .
note: The numbers do not come out whole: k = 136/9 and c = 1057/9 = 117.444..., so the intended answer is probably a round number and one of the printed constants is likely mistyped. Answer recorded as the exact consequence of the stem as printed.

stem:
In the figure, line q is parallel to line r, and both lines are intersected by line s. If y = 2x + 9, what is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The 45° angle is above q on the right of s; y is above r on the left of s. Those are not corresponding positions, so the two are not equal. Move 45° down to r as a corresponding angle (above r, right of s), then take its supplement along line r: y = 180 − 45 = 135. Now 135 = 2x + 9 gives 2x = 126 and x = 63.

whyWrong.A: 27 comes from setting y = 45 and solving 45 = 2x + 9. That treats angles on opposite sides of the transversal as equal when they are supplementary.
whyWrong.B: 73 comes from using 155 in place of 180 − 45; the supplement of 45 is 135.
whyWrong.D: 18 comes from y = 45 with a sign slip, solving 2x = 45 − 9 instead of 2x = 135 − 9.

stem:
In the figure, line p is parallel to line r, and line t intersects both lines. What is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Both marked angles sit at the same intersection, where t crosses p: x is above p on the left of t, and 72° is below p on the right of t. Angles in opposite corners of a crossing are vertical angles and are equal, so x = 72. Line r is not needed at all.

whyWrong.A: 36 is half of 72, from treating the transversal as bisecting the angle.
whyWrong.C: 180 is the straight angle along p, which is x plus the angle next to it.
whyWrong.D: 252 is 180 + 72, from adding the straight angle to the marked angle instead of matching vertical angles.

stem:
In the figure shown, line k intersects lines r and s. If w = 147, which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that lines r and s are parallel?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: To prove two lines are parallel you need a fact that is not already true regardless. w and y sit in the same position at their own intersections — both to the right of their line and above k — so they are corresponding angles, and corresponding angles are equal exactly when the lines are parallel. y = 147 = w is therefore the fact that does it.

whyWrong.A: x = 33 follows automatically from w = 147, because w and x form a straight line along r. A statement that is already true tells you nothing about s.
whyWrong.C: If w + y = 180 with w = 147, then y = 33, so the corresponding angles would differ and the lines would not be parallel.
whyWrong.D: y and z form a straight line along s, so y + z = 180 is true whatever the lines do. It never mentions r.

stem: In triangle ABC, the measure of angle A is 56° and AC = 35. In triangle PQR, the measure of angle P is 56° and PR = 105. Which additional piece of information is sufficient to prove that triangle ABC is similar to triangle PQR?

choices.label: B
choices.content: The measures of angle B and angle R are 32° and 92°, respectively.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measures of angle B and angle Q are 56° and 32°, respectively.

whyCorrect: Two triangles are similar as soon as two pairs of angles match, so look for a choice that pins down a second pair. If angle B is 32°, then angle C is 180 − 56 − 32 = 92°; and angle R is given as 92°, so angle C matches angle R while angle A already matches angle P. That is AA similarity. The side lengths 35 and 105 are a ratio of 1 to 3 and are not needed.

whyWrong.A: AB and PQ are corresponding sides, so for similarity they would have to be in the same 1 to 3 ratio as AC and PR. Equal lengths of 50 and 50 would make the triangles impossible to be similar, not similar.
whyWrong.C: This gives triangle ABC angles of 56°, 56°, 68° and triangle PQR angles of 56°, 32°, 92°. Only one pair matches, so the triangles are not similar.
whyWrong.D: AB corresponds to PQ, and QR corresponds to BC, so these two lengths are not a corresponding pair. Knowing them gives no ratio to compare with 35 to 105.

stem: In triangle RST, angle T is a right angle, point L lies on RS, point K lies on ST, and LK is parallel to RT. If the length of RT is 72 units, the length of LK is 24 units, and the area of triangle RST is 396 square units, what is the length of KT, in units?
whyCorrect: Two separate facts are needed, so take them in order. The area gives ST: \( \frac{1}{2}(72)(ST) = 396 \) , so ST = 11. Because LK is parallel to RT, triangle SLK is similar to triangle SRT with ratio \( \frac{LK}{RT} = \frac{24}{72} = \frac{1}{3} \) , so \( SK = \frac{11}{3} \) . KT is what is left of ST: \( 11 - \frac{11}{3} = \frac{22}{3} \) . The trap is stopping at SK, which is the piece the similarity gives you directly.

stem:
Which equation gives the relationship between the side lengths of the triangle shown?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: In the Pythagorean theorem the hypotenuse is always alone on one side of the equation, and the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle. Here the right-angle mark is between a and 12, so those are the legs and 14 is the hypotenuse: \( a^{2} + 12^{2} = 14^{2} \) .

whyWrong.A: This treats a as the hypotenuse. a is a leg — it touches the right angle, so it cannot be the longest side.
whyWrong.C: Side lengths in a right triangle do not add like this; the relationship is between the squares, and 12 + a is greater than 14 for the true value of a.
whyWrong.D: Adding two sides gives the third only in a degenerate flat triangle, and again a is a leg, not the sum of the others.

note: The book prints "the side length"; the figure labels three sides, so it is read as "side lengths".

stem:
In triangle XYZ, the measure of angle Y is 90 degrees. Triangle RST (not shown) is similar to triangle XYZ such that R, S, and T correspond to X, Y, and Z, respectively. Each side of triangle RST is 19 times the length of the corresponding side of triangle XYZ. What is the measure, in degrees, of one of the angles in triangle RST?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Similar triangles have identical angles no matter how the sides are scaled, so the factor of 19 changes nothing here — it is there to pull you toward multiplying. Triangle XYZ has angles 90° at Y, 35° at Z, and 180 − 90 − 35 = 55° at X, so triangle RST has those same three angles. Any one of 35, 55 or 90 answers the question.
note: Free response with three correct answers: 35, 55 and 90 are all angles of triangle RST. Recorded 35; a key listing only one of the three is still not wrong.

stem:
Triangles ABC and A′B′C′ are shown. Triangle ABC is dilated by a scale factor of 6 to form triangle A′B′C′. If the length of \( \overline{AB} \) is 18, what is the length of \( \overline{A'B'} \) ?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: A dilation multiplies every length by the scale factor, and the image here is the primed triangle, so \( A'B' = 6 \times 18 = 108 \) . The figure showing the primed triangle as the larger one confirms the direction.

whyWrong.A: 3 is 18 ÷ 6, which would be right only if the primed triangle were the original and ABC the enlargement.
whyWrong.B: 6 is the scale factor itself, not a length.
whyWrong.C: 24 is 18 + 6, adding the scale factor instead of multiplying by it.

stem: In the right triangle shown, what is the value of \( \cos A \) ?
whyCorrect: Cosine is the side next to the angle over the hypotenuse. The right angle is at B, so the hypotenuse is AC = 43, and the leg touching angle A is AB = 23. That gives \( \cos A = \frac{23}{43} \) .

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{1}{43} \) has the right denominator but a numerator of 1 instead of the adjacent leg 23.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{1}{23} \) puts the leg in the denominator and invents a 1 on top; the hypotenuse must be the denominator for a cosine.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{43}{23} \) is upside down. Any cosine is at most 1, so a value bigger than 1 cannot be right.

stem:
In triangle JKL, \( \cos y^{\circ} = \frac{54}{55} \) . What is the length of KL?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: y° is the angle at L and the right angle is at K, so KL is the leg beside y and JL is the hypotenuse: \( \cos y^{\circ} = \frac{KL}{JL} \) . The hypotenuse JL is 55, so \( \frac{KL}{55} = \frac{54}{55} \) and KL = 54. No Pythagorean work is needed — the given ratio already has 55 as its denominator.
note: In the book the length 55 is printed on top of the right-angle mark at K rather than beside a side. It must be the hypotenuse JL: reading it as the leg JK gives KL \u2248 284.5, which is not a plausible intended answer, and the parallel question on the facing page (59 with cos y = 58/59) has the same layout.

stem:
In triangle QRS, what is the value of \( \tan y^{\circ} \) ?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Tangent uses the two legs only, never the hypotenuse: opposite over adjacent. y° is at S, so the leg opposite it is QR = 4 and the leg beside it is RS = 10, giving \( \tan y^{\circ} = \frac{4}{10} \) .

whyWrong.A: c is the hypotenuse, which no tangent ever uses.
whyWrong.B: Same problem: bringing the hypotenuse in makes this a secant, not a tangent.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{10}{4} \) is opposite and adjacent swapped — it is the tangent of the angle at Q, not at S.

stem: In triangle QRS, what is the value of \( \tan y \) ?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at R, so QR = 4 and RS = 9 are the legs and c is the hypotenuse. y is the angle at S, so the opposite leg is QR = 4 and the adjacent leg is RS = 9: \( \tan y = \frac{4}{9} \) .

whyWrong.A: The hypotenuse c never appears in a tangent; this is a secant-type ratio.
whyWrong.C: Same error as A, with the other leg underneath.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{9}{4} \) reverses opposite and adjacent, giving the tangent of the angle at Q instead.

stem: In triangle JKL, \( \cos y = \frac{58}{59} \) . What is the length of KL?
whyCorrect: The right angle is at K and y is the angle at L, so the side beside y is KL and the hypotenuse is JL: \( \cos y = \frac{KL}{JL} \) . The hypotenuse is 59, so \( \frac{KL}{59} = \frac{58}{59} \) and KL = 58. The ratio is already written with the hypotenuse as its denominator, so no further computation is needed.
note: As in the companion question earlier in the chapter, the book prints the length 59 on top of the right-angle mark at K instead of beside a side; it has to be the hypotenuse JL for the numbers to work.

stem: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, where angle A corresponds to angle D and angle C corresponds to angle F. Angles C and F are right angles. If \( \tan A = \frac{612}{35} \) , what is the value of \( \sin D \) ?
whyCorrect: Similar triangles share their angles, so \( \sin D = \sin A \) and everything can be done in triangle ABC. The right angle is at C, so \( \tan A = \frac{612}{35} \) means the leg opposite A is 612 and the leg beside it is 35; the hypotenuse is \( \sqrt{612^{2} + 35^{2}} = \sqrt{375{,}769} = 613 \) . Then \( \sin A = \frac{612}{613} \) .

whyWrong.B: \( \frac{35}{613} \) is the cosine of A, built from the leg beside the angle instead of the one across from it.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{613}{612} \) is greater than 1, which no sine can be; the hypotenuse belongs underneath.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{613}{35} \) is the reciprocal of the cosine, again greater than 1.

note: This question is printed twice in the book: it also appears as Lines and Angles question 12.

stem: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, where angle A corresponds to angle D and angle C corresponds to angle F. Angles B and E are right angles. If \( \cos A = \frac{14}{\sqrt{421}} \) , what is the value of \( \frac{1}{\sin F} \) ?
whyCorrect: F corresponds to C, so \( \sin F = \sin C \) and you can work inside triangle ABC. The right angle is at B, so AC is the hypotenuse: \( \cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{14}{\sqrt{421}} \) gives AB = 14 and \( AC = \sqrt{421} \) . For angle C the opposite leg is that same AB, so \( \sin C = \frac{14}{\sqrt{421}} \) — the two acute angles swap sine and cosine. The question asks for the reciprocal, \( \frac{\sqrt{421}}{14} \) .

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{15}{\sqrt{421}} \) uses the third side, \( BC = \sqrt{421 - 196} = 15 \) ; that is \( \cos C \) , and it is not reciprocated either.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{14}{\sqrt{421}} \) is \( \sin F \) itself. The question asks for one divided by it.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{\sqrt{421}}{15} \) is the reciprocal of the cosine of F, built from the leg beside C rather than across from it.

stem:
In triangle QRS shown, QR < RS. Which expression represents the length of QS?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: QS is the hypotenuse, since the right angle is at R, and 37 is the leg RS — the one across from angle Q. So \( \sin Q = \frac{RS}{QS} = \frac{37}{QS} \) , and rearranging gives \( QS = \frac{37}{\sin Q} \) . The hypotenuse is the longest side, so the expression must divide by a sine or cosine, never multiply by one.

whyWrong.A: Multiplying by \( \cos Q \) makes the result smaller than 37, but QS is longer than either leg.
whyWrong.B: Same problem: \( \sin Q \) is less than 1, so \( 37 \sin Q \) is shorter than the leg it came from.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{37}{\cos Q} \) would be right if 37 were QR, the leg beside angle Q. 37 labels the side opposite Q, so the sine is the ratio that involves it.

note: In the book the length 37 is printed on top of the vertex label S; read as the label for side RS, the bottom leg. If it were meant for QR the answer would be C.

stem: Circles A and B are graphed in the xy-plane. Circle A is represented by the equation \( (x + 8)^{2} + (y - 8)^{2} = 64 \) and intersects the x-axis at the point (r, s). Circle B has its center at (r, s) and has a radius of the same length as circle A. Which equation represents circle B?
whyCorrect: Circle A has centre (−8, 8) and radius 8, so it just touches the x-axis. Setting y = 0 in its equation gives \( (x + 8)^{2} = 0 \) , so the only point on the x-axis is (−8, 0) — that is (r, s). Circle B therefore has centre (−8, 0) and the same radius 8: \( (x + 8)^{2} + y^{2} = 64 \) . Remember the sign flip: a centre of −8 appears as (x + 8) in the equation.

whyWrong.A: Centre (0, −8), which is on the y-axis. This swaps which coordinate the tangent point zeroed out.
whyWrong.B: Centre (0, 8) — the x- and y-coordinates of circle A's centre have been exchanged.
whyWrong.D: Centre (8, 0) has the correct y but the wrong sign on x. Circle A sits to the left of the y-axis, so r is negative.

stem: A circle in the xy-plane has its center at (−4, −7). Line k is tangent to this circle at the point (−7, −8). What is the slope of line k?
whyCorrect: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact, so find the radius's slope first and then flip it. The radius runs from (−4, −7) to (−7, −8), a slope of \( \frac{-8 - (-7)}{-7 - (-4)} = \frac{-1}{-3} = \frac{1}{3} \) . The negative reciprocal of \( \frac{1}{3} \) is −3.

whyWrong.B: \( -\frac{1}{3} \) only negates the radius's slope; a perpendicular slope must also be flipped upside down.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{1}{3} \) is the slope of the radius itself, not of the tangent.
whyWrong.D: 3 flips the fraction but keeps the sign. Perpendicular slopes must have opposite signs, since their product is −1.

stem: A circle in the xy-plane has its center at (−4, 1) and the point (−8, 4) lies on the circle. Which equation represents this circle?
whyCorrect: Two things must be right: the signs and the squaring. A centre of (−4, 1) appears in the equation as \( (x + 4)^{2} + (y - 1)^{2} \) , because the form subtracts the centre's coordinates. The radius is the distance from (−4, 1) to (−8, 4), which is \( \sqrt{(-4)^{2} + 3^{2}} = 5 \) , and the right-hand side is the radius squared, 25.

whyWrong.A: Both signs are flipped, so this is centred at (4, −1), and the right-hand side is the radius rather than its square.
whyWrong.C: The signs give a centre of (4, −1) instead of (−4, 1), though the 25 is right.
whyWrong.D: The centre is right, but 5 is the radius; the equation needs \( r^{2} \) .

stem: A piece of string with a length of 108 inches is cut into two parts. One part has a length of x inches, and the other part has a length of y inches. The value of x is 8 more than 4 times the value of y. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Write both sentences as equations: the pieces make up the whole, so x + y = 108, and "8 more than 4 times y" is x = 4y + 8. Substituting gives 4y + 8 + y = 108, so 5y = 100 and y = 20. Then x = 4(20) + 8 = 88. Check: 88 + 20 = 108.

whyWrong.A: 25 is close to y, not x, and it does not satisfy either equation; x has to be the larger piece.
whyWrong.B: 29 comes from solving 4y + 8 = 108 ÷ 4 or similar; it makes the two pieces add to far less than 108.
whyWrong.C: 58 is 108 − 50, or half of 116; check it against x = 4y + 8 — it would need y = 12.5, and then the pieces sum to 70.5.

stem: The points (0, 15), (10, 8), and (10, 3) are shown in the xy-plane, where the x-axis and y-axis are measured in units. These points define one of the bases of a triangular prism. The distance between the two bases of the prism is 20 units. What is the volume, in cubic units, of the prism?
whyCorrect: A prism's volume is the area of one base times the distance between the bases, so the only real work is the triangle's area. Two of the points share x = 10, so take that vertical segment as the base: its length is 8 − 3 = 5. The height is then the horizontal distance from the line x = 10 out to (0, 15), which is 10. The area is \( \frac{1}{2}(5)(10) = 25 \) , and the volume is 25 × 20 = 500.

stem: Rectangles ABCD and EFGH are similar. The length of each side of EFGH is 6 times the length of the corresponding side of ABCD. The area of ABCD is 90 square units. What is the area, in square units, of EFGH?
whyCorrect: Area involves two dimensions, so scaling every side by 6 scales the area by \( 6^{2} = 36 \) , not by 6. The new area is \( 90 \times 36 = 3{,}240 \) square units. You can see why with numbers: a 9 by 10 rectangle becomes 54 by 60.

whyWrong.A: 15 is 90 ÷ 6, shrinking the rectangle when the problem enlarges it.
whyWrong.B: 36 is the area scale factor by itself, with the original area never used.
whyWrong.C: 540 is 90 × 6, applying the side factor to the area. Only one of the two dimensions has been scaled.

stem: The width of a rectangle is 3 centimeters. The length of the rectangle is 20 centimeters longer than the width. What is the area, in square centimeters, of this rectangle?
whyCorrect: "20 longer than the width" means add, not multiply: the length is 3 + 20 = 23 centimeters. Area is length times width, so 23 × 3 = 69 square centimeters.

whyWrong.A: 6 is 3 + 3, or twice the width; the length was never found.
whyWrong.B: 26 is 3 + 23, the sum of the two sides rather than their product. That is half the perimeter.
whyWrong.D: 3 is the width, copied straight from the stem.

stem:
\[ h(x) = \frac{1}{2}(x)(77) \]

The given function h represents the area, in square inches, of a triangle with a base of x inches and a fixed height. What is the height, in inches, of the triangle?
whyCorrect: Match the given function against the area formula \( A = \frac{1}{2}(\text{base})(\text{height}) \) . The \( \frac{1}{2} \) is already written out and x is named as the base, so the remaining factor, 77, is the height.

whyWrong.A: \( \frac{1}{77} \) is the reciprocal of the height and does not appear in the formula at all.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{77}{2} \) folds the \( \frac{1}{2} \) into the height, but the \( \frac{1}{2} \) is a separate factor of the area formula.
whyWrong.D: 154 is 77 × 2, undoing the \( \frac{1}{2} \) as if it had already been absorbed into the 77.

stem:
The table shows the volume of two similar solids, right circular cylinder A and right circular cylinder B.

CylinderVolume (cubic units)
Right circular cylinder A\( 32\pi \)
Right circular cylinder B\( 4000\pi \)

The radius of right circular cylinder A is 4 units. The surface area of right circular cylinder A is \( k\pi \) square units, and the surface area of right circular cylinder B is \( n\pi \) square units, where k and n are constants. What is the value of \( n - k \) ? (The surface area of a right circular cylinder with radius r and height h is \( 2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi rh \) .)
whyCorrect: Get cylinder A completely, then scale. From \( \pi r^{2} h = 32\pi \) with r = 4, the height is 2, so the surface area is \( 2\pi(16) + 2\pi(4)(2) = 48\pi \) and k = 48. For similar solids the volumes are in the cube of the linear ratio: \( \frac{4000}{32} = 125 = 5^{3} \) , so B is 5 times as large in every dimension and its surface area is \( 5^{2} = 25 \) times A's. That makes \( n = 48 \times 25 = 1200 \) and \( n - k = 1152 \) .

stem: Cube B has a volume of 216 cubic inches. The length of each edge of cube A is k times the length of each edge of cube B. If cube A has a volume of 5,832 cubic inches, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: k compares edges, but the volumes are cubes of the edges, so take cube roots: \( \sqrt[3]{216} = 6 \) and \( \sqrt[3]{5{,}832} = 18 \) . Then \( k = \frac{18}{6} = 3 \) . Equivalently, the volume ratio is 27 and k is its cube root.

whyWrong.A: 27 is the ratio of the volumes, \( \frac{5{,}832}{216} \) . Edges scale by the cube root of that.
whyWrong.C: 6 is the edge length of cube B, not a ratio.
whyWrong.D: 36 is \( 6^{2} \) , the ratio of the surface areas rather than of the edges.

stem: A rectangle has an area of 48 square meters and a length of 12 meters. What is the width, in meters, of the rectangle?
whyCorrect: Area is length times width, so width is area divided by length: \( \frac{48}{12} = 4 \) meters. Check by multiplying back: 12 × 4 = 48.

whyWrong.A: 576 is 48 × 12, multiplying when you need to divide. A width cannot exceed the area's numerical value here.
whyWrong.B: 36 is 48 − 12; area and length are not combined by subtraction.
whyWrong.D: 144 is \( 12^{2} \) , the area of a square with that length, which ignores the given area.

stem: The length of the diagonal of a square is \( \frac{196\sqrt{2}}{2} \) units. What is the area, in square units, of the square?
whyCorrect: Simplify first: \( \frac{196\sqrt{2}}{2} = 98\sqrt{2} \) . A square's diagonal is \( s\sqrt{2} \) , so \( s\sqrt{2} = 98\sqrt{2} \) and s = 98. The area is \( 98^{2} = 9{,}604 \) . (You can also use \( \text{area} = \frac{d^{2}}{2} = \frac{19{,}208}{2} \) .)

whyWrong.A: 19,208 is the diagonal squared, which is twice the area — the diagonal is longer than a side.
whyWrong.B: 98 is the side length, not the area.
whyWrong.C: 392 is 4 × 98, the perimeter of the square.

stem: In triangle RST, angle T is a right angle, point L lies on RS, point K lies on ST, and LK is parallel to RT. If the length of RT is 63 units, the length of LK is 21 units, and the area of triangle RST is 630 square units, what is the length of KT, in units?
whyCorrect: Use the area to get ST first: \( \frac{1}{2}(63)(ST) = 630 \) , so ST = 20. Since LK is parallel to RT, triangle SLK is similar to triangle SRT with ratio \( \frac{21}{63} = \frac{1}{3} \) , which makes \( SK = \frac{20}{3} \) . KT is the rest of ST: \( 20 - \frac{20}{3} = \frac{40}{3} \) , about 13.33. Stopping at SK is the common slip — the similarity gives the piece next to S, not the piece next to T.
note: The book prints "If the length RT of is 63 units"; the words are transposed and are transcribed here as "the length of RT".

stem: A right square pyramid has a height of 6 units and a volume of 128 cubic units. What is the length, in units, of one side of the base of the pyramid?
whyCorrect: A pyramid's volume is \( \frac{1}{3}(\text{base area})(\text{height}) \) , and the base is a square of side s, so \( \frac{1}{3}s^{2}(6) = 128 \) . That simplifies to \( 2s^{2} = 128 \) , so \( s^{2} = 64 \) and s = 8. The last step is the one people skip: the equation gives the base area, and the side is its square root.

whyWrong.A: 256 is \( 2 \times 128 \) , from solving as though the volume were \( \frac{1}{2}s \cdot h \) ; it is also far too large for a solid of volume 128.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{64}{3} \) comes from dividing by the height without clearing the \( \frac{1}{3} \) , and it never takes the square root.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3} \) is \( \frac{8}{\sqrt{3}} \) , which appears if the \( \frac{1}{3} \) is mistakenly put inside the square root.

stem: A rectangle has an area of 66 square meters and a length of 11 meters. What is the width, in meters, of the rectangle?
whyCorrect: Width is area divided by length: \( \frac{66}{11} = 6 \) meters. Multiply back to check: 11 × 6 = 66.

whyWrong.B: 55 is 66 − 11; area and length do not subtract.
whyWrong.C: 726 is 66 × 11, multiplying instead of dividing.
whyWrong.D: 121 is \( 11^{2} \) , which ignores the given area entirely.

stem: The length of the diagonal of a square is \( \frac{186\sqrt{2}}{2} \) units. What is the area, in square units, of the square?
whyCorrect: Simplify the diagonal first: \( \frac{186\sqrt{2}}{2} = 93\sqrt{2} \) . For a square of side s the diagonal is \( s\sqrt{2} \) , so s = 93 and the area is \( 93^{2} = 8{,}649 \) .

whyWrong.B: 17,298 is the diagonal squared, which is twice the area of the square.
whyWrong.C: 93 is the side length, not the area.
whyWrong.D: 372 is 4 × 93, the perimeter.

stem: Cube B has a volume of 125 cubic inches. The length of each edge of cube A is k times the length of each edge of cube B. If cube A has a volume of 3,375 cubic inches, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Edges scale by k, so volumes scale by \( k^{3} \) . Here \( \frac{3{,}375}{125} = 27 \) , and \( k = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3 \) . Checking directly: the edges are \( \sqrt[3]{125} = 5 \) and \( \sqrt[3]{3{,}375} = 15 \) , a ratio of 3.

whyWrong.A: 27 is the volume ratio itself; the edge ratio is its cube root.
whyWrong.C: 25 is \( 5^{2} \) , cube B's face area, which is not a ratio of anything here.
whyWrong.D: 5 is cube B's edge length, not the factor connecting the two cubes.

stem: A right square pyramid has a height of 6 units and a volume of 128 cubic units. What is the length, in units, of one side of the base of the pyramid?
whyCorrect: Use \( V = \frac{1}{3}s^{2}h \) with h = 6: \( \frac{1}{3}s^{2}(6) = 2s^{2} = 128 \) , so \( s^{2} = 64 \) and the side is s = 8. Take the square root at the end — the equation solves for the base area, not the side.

whyWrong.B: 256 is twice the volume and far too large for a pyramid whose volume is only 128.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{64}{3} \) skips clearing the \( \frac{1}{3} \) and never takes a square root.
whyWrong.D: \( \frac{8\sqrt{3}}{3} \) equals \( \frac{8}{\sqrt{3}} \) , which comes from leaving the 3 under the radical.

note: This question is printed twice on the same page, as items 14 and 18, with the choices reordered.

stem: A triangle has a base length of 48 centimeters and a height of 96 centimeters. What is the area, in square centimeters, of the triangle?
whyCorrect: Area of a triangle is \( \frac{1}{2}(\text{base})(\text{height}) = \frac{1}{2}(48)(96) \) . Halve 48 first to keep it simple: 24 × 96 = 2,304 square centimeters.

whyWrong.B: 1152 halves twice — it is \( \frac{1}{2} \) of the correct area.
whyWrong.C: 4608 is 48 × 96, the rectangle's area, with the \( \frac{1}{2} \) forgotten.
whyWrong.D: 144 is 48 + 96, adding the dimensions instead of multiplying.

stem: A right circular cylinder has a height of 16 inches and a volume of \( 3136\pi \) cubic inches. What is the radius, in inches, of this cylinder?
whyCorrect: Use \( V = \pi r^{2} h \) . The \( \pi \) cancels on both sides, leaving \( 16r^{2} = 3136 \) , so \( r^{2} = 196 \) and r = 14. Remember the final square root: \( r^{2} \) is 196, which is not the answer.

stem: The length of a side of square X is 9 centimeters. The area of rectangle Y is 32 square centimeters. What is the total area, in square centimeters, of square X and rectangle Y?
whyCorrect: The 9 is a side, not an area, so square it first: square X has area \( 9^{2} = 81 \) square centimeters. Adding rectangle Y's 32 gives 81 + 32 = 113.

whyWrong.A: 145 comes from using 4 × 9 = 36 (the perimeter) plus... more simply, it is 113 + 32, adding Y's area twice.
whyWrong.C: 82 adds the side length 9 to 32 and then adds 41 again; more directly, it treats the square's area as 50. The square's area is 81.
whyWrong.D: 81 is square X's area alone, with rectangle Y left out.

stem:
Kyle invented a new temperature scale he called the Tutorllini scale. The function T(x) gives the temperature, in degrees Torte, that corresponds to a temperature of x degrees Celsius.

\[ T(x) = \frac{3}{4}\left(\frac{26x}{7} - 800\right) + 15.50 \]

If a temperature increased by 3.3 degrees Torte, by how much did the temperature increase, in degrees Celsius?
whyCorrect: Only the rate of change matters, so ignore every constant. Expanding, the coefficient of x is \( \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{26}{7} = \frac{39}{14} \) , meaning each Celsius degree is worth \( \frac{39}{14} \) Torte degrees. To find the Celsius change that produces 3.3 Torte, divide rather than multiply: \( 3.3 \div \frac{39}{14} = \frac{33}{10} \cdot \frac{14}{39} = \frac{77}{65} \approx 1.185 \) . The −800 and the +15.50 shift the scale but never change how fast it moves.
note: The answer is not a round number: 77/65 = 1.1846..., so a grid entry would be 77/65 or 1.18/1.19.

stem:
In the given system of equations, p is a constant. If the system has no solution, what is the value of p?

\[ \frac{3}{2}y - \frac{1}{4}x = \frac{2}{3} - \frac{3}{2}y \]
\[ \frac{1}{6}x + \frac{3}{6} = py + \frac{9}{5} \]
whyCorrect: No solution means the two lines are parallel: the x and y coefficients are in the same ratio while the constants are not. Put both equations in the form \( ax + by = c \) first. The first becomes \( -\frac{1}{4}x + 3y = \frac{2}{3} \) once the \( \frac{3}{2}y \) is brought across; the second becomes \( \frac{1}{6}x - py = \frac{13}{10} \) . Matching x-coefficients, \( \frac{1}{6} \div \left(-\frac{1}{4}\right) = -\frac{2}{3} \) , so the y-coefficients must satisfy \( -p = 3\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) = -2 \) , giving p = 2. The constants do not follow the same ratio, so the lines really are parallel and not identical.

stem:
In the given system of equations, t is a constant. If the system has no solution, what is the value of t?

\[ 4x - 6y = 10y + 2 \]
\[ ty = \frac{1}{2} + 2x \]
whyCorrect: Collect the variables on one side of each equation before comparing anything. The first becomes \( 4x - 16y = 2 \) , the second \( -2x + ty = \frac{1}{2} \) . For no solution the coefficient pairs must be proportional: the x-coefficients scale by \( \frac{-2}{4} = -\frac{1}{2} \) , so \( t = -16 \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = 8 \) . Check the constants: \( 2 \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -1 \) , which is not \( \frac{1}{2} \) , so the lines are parallel rather than the same line.

stem:
\[ \frac{20}{p} = \frac{20}{q} - \frac{20}{r} - \frac{20}{s} \]

The given equation relates the positive variables p, q, r, and s. Which of the following is equivalent to q?
whyCorrect: Every term carries a 20, so divide it out at once: \( \frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{q} - \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{s} \) . Isolate the reciprocal of q rather than q itself: \( \frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{s} = \frac{rs + ps + pr}{prs} \) . Only now take reciprocals of both sides, giving \( q = \frac{prs}{pr + rs + ps} \) .

whyWrong.A: This is what you get by reading \( \frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{s} \) as q = p + r + s. Reciprocals do not distribute over addition.
whyWrong.B: Same error, with the 20 kept even though it cancels from every term.
whyWrong.D: The 20s cancel completely, so leaving three of them in the denominator makes this 20 times too small.
